description: we are doing a web site of SPHEREX
summary:
SPHEREx Time Machine is a free web tool that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey into a time-lapse of any spot in the sky. Type coordinates or a name, and the page finds every SPHEREx exposure that covers that spot. It then reads only the small piece it needs straight from NASA’s public archive and lines all the frames up with north at the top, so whatever moves or changes stands out when you press play.

The tool covers what the challenge asks for:

Comparing frames: blink and difference modes, and a marker that follows fast-moving stars.
Adding images together: per detector, or season by season.
Catalogues and warnings: Gaia and WISE stars drawn over the image, plus NASA’s own warnings for doubtful pixels.
Measuring: spectra and brightness-over-time curves.
Sharing: links that carry the coordinates and can be embedded in another page.

A robot on GitHub checks the archive every day, so new releases appear on their own.

We tested it on all five challenge objects. By adding 43 exposures together, it reveals WISE 0855−0714, a brown dwarf too faint to see in a single frame.

This matters because SPHEREx data is huge and hard to use. This tool lets students, teachers and the public explore real NASA data in English or Spanish, with no installation and no server of our own.
details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREx Time Machine is a web page that plays NASA SPHEREx images of any spot in the sky as a time-lapse. You type coordinates (in almost any format) or the name of an object, and the page answers in a few seconds:

  1. It finds the images. A small “pointing index” that we built records where SPHEREx looked in all 1.6 million released images. A search over it takes under a second, right in the browser.
  2. It downloads only what it needs. From NASA’s public archive on AWS, the browser reads just the strip of each 70 MB file that contains the target, about 1 MB per image.
  3. It lines the frames up. Using the position data stored in each file, every frame is turned so north is up, at the same scale, so anything that jumps between frames really moved in the sky.
  4. It follows fast stars. For a star with a known motion across the sky, the page works out where it is today and marks where it should be in every frame.

Viewer tools:

  • Play, pause and step through frames; zoom, pan, and save the image.
  • Blink and Difference modes to compare two dates.
  • Adding exposures together per detector, or season by season, so faint objects appear.
  • Spectra (brightness against colour) and light curves (brightness against date).
  • Gaia and WISE catalogue stars drawn over the image.
  • NASA’s per-pixel quality warnings painted over the image (cosmic-ray hits, satellite streaks, saturation).
  • Links that carry the coordinates, and an embed mode for other websites.
  • A switch between English and Spanish.

A GitHub Action checks NASA’s archive every day and updates the index on its own, so new data releases appear without anyone editing anything.

Benefits

  • No installation, no account and no server of our own. It works on a phone, and 37 saved targets work even without internet.
  • Every pixel is real NASA data, and every frame links to its original file, so anyone can check it.
  • We tested it on all five challenge objects. Barnard’s Star visibly moves north, and RW Aurigae dims over a year. WISE 0855−0714 is too faint to see in one frame, but adding 43 exposures together makes it appear 20 times above the noise, exactly where its motion predicts.

Intended impact

SPHEREx data is huge and hard to use: millions of 70 MB files and specialised software. We want students, teachers, amateur astronomers and citizen scientists to explore it and notice things that move or change, such as nearby stars, asteroids and variable stars. The Spanish version opens it to Latin American schools.

Tools and languages

  • Web page: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in a single page with no framework. It reads the FITS image files, their position data, wavelength tables and compressed quality layers directly in the browser.
  • Build scripts: Python, using only the standard library plus Astropy and NumPy.
  • Hosting and automation: GitHub Pages hosts the site, and GitHub Actions runs the daily index refresh.
    • NASA/IPAC IRSA and its public SPHEREx bucket on AWS (the images)
    • CDS SIMBAD (names and motions)
    • CDS VizieR (Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues)
    • JPL Horizons (positions of planets and asteroids)
    • a link to Aladin Lite
  • Hardware: a personal laptop.
  • AI: developed with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

Creativity

  • Instead of relying on a slow archive search, we built our own index from the telescope’s fixed camera layout. One pointing per exposure is enough to predict, to a fraction of a pixel, which of the six detectors sees a target.
  • The page is opened by a wall of real SPHEREx frames that keep changing dates.
  • The tool shows that faint objects are hidden in the data, and lets users reveal them by adding images together.

What we considered

  • Honesty: only real data, with clear warnings where a measurement is rough.
  • Ease of use: the coordinate search sits on its own tab, and every control has a “?” explanation.
  • Low download size, so it works on slow connections.
  • Accessibility, phone screens, light and dark themes, and two languages.
  • Staying current automatically as NASA releases new data.
